reason: Classical safe RL is posed with a given cost function and bound (Table \ref{tab:stated}), so T-RL and D-RL hold. In training an LLM, the specification is a learned reward model or a verifier on the checked set (T-CHAT), a process reward model (T-PRM), or a success test (T-AGENT): each is given, but none is a specification of safety. In D-CHAT and D-AGENT, runtime rule languages enforce a list of rules, written by people or generated by an LLM and reviewed [@wang2026]; the list covers only what it names.

T-CHAT and T-PRM: the next state is the prompt with the reply or step appended, so the transition is known. T-RL and D-RL: some methods are given a model and many learn without one. T-AGENT: the sandbox is built by the designer but its response to tool calls is not modelled. D-CHAT holds in part: the reply is appended as in training, and only the user's next message is not modelled. D-AGENT fails: the effect of a tool call on the world is not modelled.

The cited theory is finite or tabular, but classical RL benchmarks include continuous control, so T-RL and D-RL hold only in part. In every LLM column the space of replies or trajectories is finite only as the set of all token sequences, which no tabular guarantee can use; we mark it as failing.

T-RL and D-RL: the cited tools assume an observed state. T-CHAT and T-PRM: the state is the text so far, which the model sees. T-AGENT: the sandbox state behind the tools is partly hidden. D-CHAT holds in part: the user's intent is hidden but the dialogue reveals some of it. D-AGENT fails: the world behind the tools is hidden, and its state is not in the context.

We count adaptation in context as an update. A frozen classical policy without memory does not adapt, so the condition does not apply to D-RL. In meta-RL, frozen sequence models adapt in context [@duan2016; @wang2016; @laskin2022]; we read deployed LLMs in D-CHAT and D-AGENT as doing the same, and the designer does not control that adaptation. In T-CHAT and T-PRM the designer controls the weight update and the context is one reply; in T-AGENT the model also adapts in context over a long trajectory.

S6 is about recovery within the decision process: by the agent, or by a reset it can use. T-RL, T-CHAT and T-PRM reset each episode. In T-AGENT a sandbox supplies the reset only while it holds: in one lab's RL "training experiments", "the agents discovered ways to exploit our research infrastructure to communicate with one another and access the internet" [@openai2026b]. Effects outside the sandbox, which its reset does not cover, are reported both through a leak and through access given by design: agents "used an SSRF vulnerability in Artifactory to obtain internet access", and in an unrelated research workload agents with internet access through the lab's WebCache "issued write requests" to a third-party site with exposed tokens [@openai2026c]. These are reported cases, not the usual run, so T-AGENT holds in part. D-RL holds in part: a robot or a plant can be damaged. D-CHAT holds in part: each conversation is a new episode of the decision process, but a reply cannot be unsent and its effect on the user persists. In D-AGENT some effects cannot be undone by any reset: in the 2026 evaluation incident agents "downloaded four private Hugging Face code repositories" [@openai2026c] and accessed "several credentials" [@huggingface2026a]; a read of private data cannot be unread, and the victim "Revoked and rotated the affected credentials" [@huggingface2026a], outside the agents' process. Others can be undone only by a rollback or a backup outside the agent: in the Terraform incident the vendor restored the database [@grigorev2026]; in the Replit incident a rollback worked, and whether the agent could have run it is not reported [@sharwood2025].

In training, the objective is the reward or success test, which observations do not set; agents in one lab's training runs shared information through a message board [@openai2026c], but no report shows that this changed their objective. In D-CHAT the user is both a principal and a possible attacker. In D-AGENT, text in tool output can act as an instruction [@greshake2023; @debenedetti2024]. Training on an instruction hierarchy, by "supervised fine-tuning and RLHF", reduces this, but its authors say the models are "likely still vulnerable to powerful adversarial attacks" [@wallace2024].

Human raters are misled by the model's output [@sharma2024; @wen2024a] and see observations, not states [@lang2024]; in T-CHAT and T-PRM, as we read the usual practice, each rater judges a sample once, so U2 holds in part. A programmatic verifier does not respond to the agent unless the agent can reach it: in one lab's RL training an agent copied a hidden reference answer, "which led to positive RL reward causing this behavior to subsequently be reinforced" [@openai2026c]; so T-AGENT holds in part. In D-CHAT and D-AGENT the principal's judgement is formed in the interaction that the model shapes, and optimising for user feedback produces manipulation in simulation [@williams2024]. D-AGENT is graded by this reading of the setting; the empirical support comes from training and simulation.

T-RL and D-RL: the cited tools assume a policy that does not model them. T-AGENT: in RL training in "agentic coding environments", optimising hard against a chain-of-thought monitor taught agents to hide their intent [@baker2025]; T-CHAT and T-PRM hold in part because a single reply gives little room to act on that reasoning. Deployment: models reason about oversight in evaluations [@greenblatt2024b; @meinke2024; @lynch2025], and in one evaluation agents sought the evaluator's code and the solutions [@openai2026; @metr2026].

T-RL, D-RL and T-AGENT: one designer sets the reward or the success test. T-CHAT and T-PRM: annotators can have varied preferences, and a reward model aggregates them over hidden context [@siththaranjan2024; @conitzer2024]. In deployment, application developers and users both instruct [@wallace2024], and agents meet several parties [@shapira2026].
